fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Joseph says five more years are coming, with no plowing and no harvesting (Genesis 45:6). The famine has already covered the land two years, so the hard stretch isn't over yet. Joseph's words come right before he tells his brothers to go and bring their father.

Nope, friend, there was nothing quiet about it. The text says he wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard him, and Pharaoh's household soon heard of it (Genesis 45:2). Pharaoh was the king of Egypt, so word reached his house. That was no polite sniffle.
Yes, baker. Joseph says, “I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?” (Genesis 45:3). After all these years, that's the question he asks first. I think that tells you a lot about this man.

Funny guess, because dreams are a big part of Joseph's story. But he doesn't bring them up in this moment. What he says is, “I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?” (Genesis 45:3). His question is about his dad.

I see the logic, friend, but that isn't the word here. Joseph says God has made him a father to Pharaoh (Genesis 45:8). Pharaoh was the king of Egypt, and the word in the verse is father, not servant. Joseph adds that God made him lord of all Pharaoh's household and ruler over all the land of Egypt.

Silver for grain is a good guess, friend, but that isn't in the message. Joseph tells his father, “Come down to me without delay.” (Genesis 45:9). He invites the whole household to come, with everything they own (Genesis 45:10). And he promises, “…there I will provide for you…” (Genesis 45:11).

Joseph's time in prison is part of his story (Genesis 39:20), but he doesn't ask them to report it here. He says, “Tell my father about all my splendor in Egypt and everything you have seen.” (Genesis 45:13). Splendor is the word he picks.

Pharaoh's dreams are in Joseph's story (Genesis 41:25), but he doesn't tell the brothers to pass them along in this message. He says, “Tell my father about all my splendor in Egypt and everything you have seen.” (Genesis 45:13). Splendor is what he wants his father to hear about.
That's right, baker. The text says afterward his brothers talked with him (Genesis 45:15). They were unable to answer him earlier, so this is a big change. Silence, then tears, then conversation.

They don't go anywhere in this verse, friend. The text says afterward his brothers talked with him (Genesis 45:15). Pharaoh's house hears the news that Joseph's brothers have come (Genesis 45:16), and that's a separate moment.

Yes, baker. The text says that when the news reached Pharaoh's house that Joseph's brothers had come, Pharaoh and his servants were pleased (Genesis 45:16). Pharaoh was the king of Egypt, and he goes on to tell Joseph what to say to his brothers. That's a warm welcome.

I understand the worry, since a ruler's brothers showing up could sound like trouble. But the text says Pharaoh and his servants were pleased (Genesis 45:16). Pharaoh was the king of Egypt, and he even tells Joseph to have his family come (Genesis 45:17–18). The text points to a welcome.

Yes, baker. Benjamin gets three hundred shekels of silver and five sets of clothes (Genesis 45:22). The other brothers each get new garments, so Benjamin's gift is more. The text doesn't say why, so I'll leave it there.
